processing: Simple infusion of fresh or dried shiso leaf; nothing more than picking, stemming and, for keeping, drying.
harvest_season: Summer, when shiso is in leaf; dried leaf is available all year.
appearance_dry: Crumbled, dark green or purple-brown leaf when dried; soft, whole leaves when fresh.
appearance_liquor: Pale green-yellow from green shiso; red shiso gives a dusky tint that turns bright purple-pink with acid.
taste_profile: Fresh and herbal with the familiar minty, basil-like shiso scent; red leaf is a little spicier.

brewing.notes: Tear stemmed fresh leaves into a pot, pour on boiling water and wait about three minutes. A squeeze of citrus turns a red shiso brew brighter.

vintage_note: Fresh shiso tea is a summer home drink with no market at all; dried leaf and tea bags sell all year with no vintage. As with other dried herbs, buy recent stock, since the aroma fades.
description:
Shiso tea is the plainest idea on this list: the herb that sits beside your sashimi, in hot water. Green or red perilla leaf both work, and many people simply make it from garden leaves.

There is barely any processing. Pull the stems, tear the leaves and pour on boiling water, or dry a summer glut for later. The colour is the fun part with red shiso, whose pigment shifts to a vivid purple-pink once acid goes in.

It tastes as the leaf smells, green, minty and a little peppery, and it is refreshing both hot and cold. Red shiso leans spicier. Don't overdo the steep if you find the herb assertive.

This is more a home habit than a trade product, so there are no grades to learn. If you buy it dried, look for good colour and a strong smell when you open the bag.
history: Little is documented about shiso tea as a named drink. It sits within the wider everyday use of perilla as a culinary herb in Japan and elsewhere in East Asia, and it remains mostly a home preparation. Health claims attached to it, such as lowering cholesterol, are unproven.
